messages.content: What's the total number of possible arrangements in a chess game?

message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that the “Shannon number” – a lower bound on the size of the game tree – is on the order of

\[
10^{43}\text{–}10^{50}
\]

legal positions.

More recent computational work has refined this estimate.  The most widely cited figure is that there are roughly

\[
\boxed{10^{43}\text{ legal positions}}
\]

(about 43 digits).  If you include all *possible* arrangements of the 32 pieces on the board, even those that would never occur in a legal game, the count rises to roughly

\[
\boxed{10^{46}\text{–}10^{47}\text{ total arrangements}}
\]

So, in short, there are on the order of ten‑to‑the‑forty‑third legal positions in chess.
